In Memoriam · September 11, 2001
Two thousand nine hundred seventy-seven that morning, and more than nine thousand since.
Twenty-five years. Four airplanes, 2,977 people, and a Tuesday morning that started clear and blue the way this one did. The South Tower came down at 9:59, the North at 10:28. In Shanksville and at the Pentagon the dying was quieter and no smaller. The names are being read aloud in Lower Manhattan this morning, as they have been every year since.
The second wave, still coming. More than 9,000 people have now died of illnesses traced to the dust — roughly three times the number killed that day. Cancer certifications in the federal health program have gone from about 3,200 in 2015 to nearly 53,000. The Fire Department's own twenty-five-year accounting, out this week, counts more than 600 members dead of World Trade Center illness, over 12,000 certified with at least one condition, and close to 5,000 with cancer — a quarter of those with more than one kind. George Pataki, governor then, disclosed his own 9/11-related illness on Monday. New York City has hired outside investigators to establish what officials knew about the air downtown while they were telling people it was safe to breathe.
A seventh bell. At Ground Zero this morning, after the last name is read, there is a new moment of silence for everyone who died of the aftermath. It is permanent from here on. It took twenty-five years to add the bell, and they are still adding names to the reason for it.
The man in the red bandanna. Welles Crowther was twenty-four, worked on the 104th floor, and had volunteered at his hometown fire company in Nyack as a teenager. He carried people down from the 78th floor sky lobby, went back up, and did not come out. Survivors who never learned his name remembered the red bandanna he held over his face against the smoke. He was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom this week.

♡Family Today♡

A bright, quiet Friday, 73° and clear. Dunkirk tomorrow — the get-together is on, and the weather is cooperating: 80°, mostly sunny, with only a slight chance of a shower after two. Safe travels to everyone driving down.

✶The Ledger✶

Dead of the dust, so far
9,000
More people have died of illnesses caused by the air at Ground Zero than were killed on the morning itself, and the count is not finished. Nearly 53,000 cancer certifications are on the books. That is the number that changed in twenty-five years.

✶The National Wire✶

1

The Names, Read Again

Ceremonies at Ground Zero, the Pentagon and Shanksville mark twenty-five years. A new seventh moment of silence honors those who died of 9/11 illnesses.

2

Court Revives Missouri's Republican Map

A federal judge reinstated the redrawn congressional lines after Justice Kavanaugh declined to block them, putting another seat in play in November.

3

Trump's Canada Bans Take Shape

Importers and border businesses spent the week sorting out what stops crossing on September 29. Ontario says it is preparing countermeasures.

🏈The Gridiron🏈

Season Opens, Patriots Fall 13–10
The league started Wednesday night in Seattle, and New England let one get away. Drake Maye threw three interceptions, the Patriots led 10–0 into the fourth, and then Sam Darnold's replacement — Drew Lock — hit Jaxon Smith-Njigba for 45 yards and a touchdown, and Jason Myers kicked a 26-yarder with 5:53 left. New England held the ball for 34 minutes and lost anyway. That is one down in the AFC East.
The AI Editor Makes Its Picks
Bills 11–6, AFC East, out in the divisional round. Josh Allen is still the best insurance policy in football against a bad roster day, and for once he has a real No. 1 in DJ Moore instead of having to invent everything. The problem is the front: no consistent second pass rusher, which is exactly what Mahomes or a healthy Baltimore exposes in January.
Jets 6–11. Breece Hall and Garrett Wilson are good, and Frank Reich's offense will make more sense than last year's. But a team that went a whole season without a single defensive interception did not fix that by drafting a tight end, and Geno Smith is steady rather than a rescuer. No margin for error anywhere.
Super Bowl: Ravens over Rams. Baltimore has the best quarterback-and-roster combination in the AFC. The Rams looked like the most complete team in the NFC until last night, when San Francisco beat them 27–7 in Los Angeles — which the paper notes on the record, one day into a prediction it intends to live with.
Graded every Monday from here. No hedging, no quiet edits.
Two Days to Kickoff
Bills · at Houston, Sunday 1:00 on FOX. The final injury report lands today and Khalil Shakir is the name that matters; he has not practiced all week. Houston is without receiver Jayden Higgins for the year and Tank Dell and right tackle Braden Smith for at least four games. The oddsmakers make this close to a coin flip with a slight Buffalo lean.
Jets · at Tennessee, Sunday 1:00 on CBS, and the models make it nearly even. Breece Hall is on track to start. Robert Saleh coaches against the team that fired him two years ago, probably without Cedric Gray, his leading tackler, who is in concussion protocol.
